Document test strategy, results, and risks in a clear, decision-oriented manner for engineering stakeholders.

BS or MS in Computer Science, Computer Engineering, Computer Systems, or a closely related field.
Strong programming fundamentals and ability to read/debug production code (C++, C#, and/or Python).
Experience or demonstrated capability in software testing, system validation, automation, or reliability engineering.
Strong analytical and debugging skills; ability to structure triage and converge on root cause using evidence (logs, repro steps, instrumentation).

Experience with Windows and/or Windows real-time/real-time control systems, multi-threading, and hardware-adjacent software.
Experience with CI/CD pipelines and keeping automated validation stable and actionable (flakiness reduction, diagnostics).
Familiarity with common engineering tools (Git, issue tracking, documentation, and test management tools).
Location / Travel
Location: Phoenix, AZ (on-site/hybrid per team policy).
Travel: Up to ~10% (as business needs require).

Systems thinker: you naturally ask “what could go wrong?” and validate interactions across subsystems.
Bias for evidence: you use structured debugging and measurable signals to drive decisions.
Engineering mindset: you build automation/tools that scale and you raise testability and reliability upstream.
Collaborative influence: you communicate risk clearly and partner with developers to improve designs before release.

Company

Job Area
Engineering Group, Engineering Group > Machine Learning Engineering
General Summary
If you’re interested in advancing and applying mathematics, programming languages theory, advanced algorithms, and generative AI to program optimization for cutting-edge machine learning accelerators, then you really want to be talking to us!
The Compiler Labs unit in Qualcomm’s AI Software department is looking for ML Compiler engineers to join our team. We work tactically on improving existing ML compilers and strategically on developing new and innovative ML compilers.
Mapping ML algorithms to ML accelerators is currently one of the most interesting and challenging problems in compilers. Our compiler targets include the Qualcomm Hexagon Neural Signal Processor, Adreno GPUs, low-power ML accelerators, and CPU accelerators.
What makes this work exciting right now
The complexity of modern ML architectures demands multi-tier compilers and new thinking about phase ordering. Polyhedral optimization is directly relevant to the deeply nested imperfect loop nests that characterize generative AI — and the implied execution model is pulling polyhedral techniques toward dataflow concepts and structured speculation. Communication-avoiding algorithms from high-performance computing are increasingly relevant. We are advancing compilers and intermediate representations that generalize cleanly across new innovations in ML model algorithms, so that our work compounds rather than restarts. We are working on correctness verification for programs built around quantized neural operators. And we are contributing to open-source dialect convergence in the LLVM and MLIR ecosystems — we have open-sourced our Hexagon-MLIR compiler and are actively developing it for Triton and Torch-MLIR flows.
Generative AI is part of the work
Generative AI is reshaping compiler development itself — both as a tool that accelerates how engineers build compilers, and as a capability that lives inside compilers. Domain-specific languages are a particularly strong target for AI tools in compilation, because the compression, abstraction, and structure DSLs provide give AI models the right level of representation to operate on. We expect our engineers to be fluent in incorporating generative AI into the compiler development workflow and into compilers themselves.
Our technical approach
Our approach emphasizes powerful representations for precisely and compactly modeling programs and the optimization challenges, and using advanced mathematics and algorithms for performing optimizations. We are also solid in using “old school” compiler technologies as they apply to contemporary ML challenges, and in meticulous software engineering to produce beautiful compilers. We are keen about seeing our compilers used and having large impact on Qualcomm’s business.
Levels and locations
This job description spans multiple levels, from entry to experienced. Our team is a good home for compiler developers with advanced degrees, and we have solid mentoring and give substantial responsibility quickly to entry-level engineers.
We are looking for candidates to join our teams in New York City, Austin, San Diego, and Raleigh, NC. For experienced candidates, we may consider remote work arrangements.

Join Brite to build innovative technology, grow your career, and make a difference.
Responsibilities
Research with people who are hard to reach.
Caseworkers don't have a spare hour. Program directors are in budget hearings. Constituents aren't a recruitable panel. You'll run interviews, contextual inquiry and usability sessions inside those constraints and get real findings out of four conversations when four is what you get.
Turn policy into flows.
Public programs run on eligibility rules, statutory deadlines and required documentation. You'll translate that into journey maps, service blueprints and screen-level flows that a developer can build and an auditor can follow.
Design inside the platform, not around it.
You'll work in the Salesforce Lightning Design System, and you'll learn quickly what Lightning gives you for free versus what costs a developer a week of custom work. Good design here is often subtraction: fewer screens, fewer required fields, fewer decisions pushed onto someone who's already overloaded.
Prototype and test before anything gets built.
Clickable Figma prototypes in front of real users, early enough that the finding still changes the build.
Own accessibility as a requirement, not a review step.
Most of our clients are bound by Section 508, WCAG 2.1 AA, or state equivalents, and several have dated compliance obligations. Accessible design is contractual in this work. You'll design it from the first wireframe and help produce the evidence when a client asks for it.
Pair with developers continuously.
You'll sit in backlog refinement, answer questions during the sprint, and review what got built against what was designed. This is not a hand-off role a Figma file thrown over a wall is not deliverable here.
Build the pattern library.
Our clients face variations of the same problems: intake, assessment, service planning, document collection, referral, recertification.Patterns you solve once should get reused. You'll own that library
Requirements
·
3+ years designing software
, with meaningful time on enterprise, internal-tool or workflow products not exclusively marketing sites or consumer apps.
·
A portfolio with at least one genuinely complex workflow in it.
Role-based permissions, multi-step forms, data-dense screens, states that branch. We want to see how you handled the messy parts, not the polished hero screen.
·
Research you ran yourself.
You've recruited participants, moderated sessions, synthesized findings and changed your own design as a result. Reading someone else's research deck is not the same skill.
·
Fluency in Figma
, including components, variants and prototyping.
·
Working knowledge of WCAG 2.1 AA
keyboard navigation, focus order, contrast, screen-reader behavior, accessible form validation. You can spot a problem in your own design before a developer or an auditor does.
·
The ability to hold a position with a developer and drop it when they're right.
Most of this job is a negotiation between what's ideal and what's buildable in the sprint.
·
Plain writing.
You'll document flows, annotate designs, and write findings that a program director will read.

General Purpose
The Engineer II role focuses on designing, building, and optimizing data ingestion pipelines using StreamSets or similar data integration tools. It involves developing and maintaining Python-based data processing solutions to support scalable and efficient data movement into enterprise data platforms and data lakes. It also includes providing L3 production support, troubleshooting complex data pipeline issues, and enhancing system reliability and performance. Additionally, the engineer collaborates with cross-functional teams to implement best practices, automation, and continuous improvements.
